key_findings.finding: Direct human evidence supports an association between impaired fibrinolysis and persistent perfusion defects after acute PE: in a 71-patient follow-up study at 1 year (off anticoagulation), patients with ≥10% scintigraphic residual perfusion defects (n=18) had significantly longer clot-lysis time (p<0.05) and higher PAI-1 (p<0.01) than those with <10% defects (n=53); lysis time and time-to-diagnosis were independently associated with ≥10% defects in multivariable logistic regression (p<0.001). No pulmonary hypertension was present, so this pertains to residual defects rather than established CTEPH.

A prospective observational study of 79 normotensive, noncancer acute-PE patients assessed at admission, 5–7 days, and 3 months, with CT angiographic RPVO at 3–6 months, found RPVO in 23/79 (29.1%). RPVO patients had denser fibrin clots (lower fibrin-clot permeability Ks, p<0.001) and longer clot-lysis time (p<0.05) at baseline and day 5–7; baseline Ks, baseline D-dimer, and 3-month E-selectin were independently associated with RPVO. This supports an association with hypofibrinolytic/prothrombotic clot phenotype, although CLT was not independently reported as an RPVO predictor and the study was not designed to establish causality.

Evidence is not uniformly positive: an ancillary analysis of the PADIS-PE randomized trial included only 23 adults with first unprovoked PE and initial pulmonary vascular obstruction ≥30%; after anticoagulation and warfarin discontinuation, 6 (26%) had RPVO ≥5%. Quantitative D-dimer, tPA, uPA, TFPI and a tissue-factor-based turbidimetric clot-lysis assay were measured, but clot formation/lysis parameters were not associated with RPVO. TGFβ1, not the fibrinolysis measures, was higher in RPVO. Thus, this small study does not replicate the direct fibrinolysis-RPVO association.

A prospective cross-sectional genetic study compared 46 Turkish CTEPH patients with 106 healthy volunteers and found association of the fibrinogen Aα THR312ALA polymorphism with CTEPH (e.g., THR/ALA vs ALA/ALA susceptibility OR 5.026, 95% CI 1.774–14.242; THR/THR vs ALA/THR showed lower susceptibility). VKORC1 and CYP2C9 polymorphisms were not associated. This is indirect thrombophilia/fibrin-structure evidence in established CTEPH, not a direct assay of impaired fibrinolytic capacity or a longitudinal demonstration after acute PE.

Overall conclusion: residual pulmonary perfusion defects/RPVO after PE are plausibly and in several human cohorts associated with impaired fibrinolytic capacity—especially prolonged clot-lysis time, elevated PAI-1, and dense/less permeable fibrin clots—but the evidence base is small, heterogeneous, and partly conflicting. Direct evidence is strongest for residual defects without pulmonary hypertension; evidence in established CTEPH is more indirect and genetic/structural, and available studies do not establish that hypofibrinolysis causes persistent obstruction.
